hook: From the first hours of the war on a quiet North Atlantic evening in September nineteen thirty-nine, to a small grey U-boat raising a black flag in the western approaches in May nineteen forty-five, the long Battle of the Atlantic, told softly, so you can rest.
narration:
Imagine you are standing on the open bridge wing of a small corvette in the middle of the North Atlantic in the spring of nineteen forty-three. The night is dark. The wind is on the port bow at force seven. The corvette, a four-stack-funnel ship of fourteen hundred tons, lifts on a long grey swell, hangs for a moment with her propeller half out of the water, and drops into the trough beyond. Cold spray comes over the wheelhouse and freezes in your beard. Somewhere to starboard, a row of dim blue stern lights traces the long shape of a convoy of forty merchant ships, plodding eastward at seven and a half knots toward the British Isles. From below your feet, in the small steel asdic hut on the bridge, comes the slow steady ping of the underwater listening set, a sound between a chime and a heartbeat. Once every five seconds it goes out into the cold black water, and once every five seconds it comes back unanswered. The date is the second of April, nineteen forty-three. Somewhere out there, in the long dark below, ten or fifteen German U-boats are listening for you. You have not yet heard their engines.

Tonight, we will follow the long Battle of the Atlantic from this dark bridge wing all the way back to the first hours of the war in September nineteen thirty-nine, and forward to the spring of nineteen forty-five, when the last U-boats surface to surrender. There is no urgency in this story. The years will pass at their own pace. The names of the ships and the convoys and the men will pass through the narrative as they came, and they will not be tested. You are welcome to drift, to come and go, to fall asleep at any time. The story will keep itself.

A word, before we begin, about what kind of battle this is. The films of later years, and the paperback covers, will give you the U-boat aces — Prien and Schepke and Kretschmer — leaning on their conning towers in the Atlantic dawn, with their white officer's caps and their sleek long boats. They were real. But the war was not won, in the end, by aces. It was won by long, patient, often boring work — by men in small ships standing the middle watch in fog, by mathematicians in a country house in Buckinghamshire reading German radio traffic, by riveters in shipyards in Baltimore and on the Clyde, by aircraft crews flying very long sorties over very empty water. The Battle of the Atlantic is the longest battle of the Second World War. It begins on the first day. It ends on the last. We will follow it, slowly, from one end to the other.

On the evening of the third of September, nineteen thirty-nine, a few hours after the British Prime Minister, Neville Chamberlain, has announced from the Downing Street cabinet room that a state of war exists between Britain and Germany, the passenger liner Athenia, of the Anchor-Donaldson Line, bound from Liverpool for Montreal with twelve hundred and three souls aboard, is moving westward through the dusk two hundred and fifty miles northwest of Ireland. The Atlantic is mild, almost calm. A few children are on the boat deck watching the wake. At seven thirty-eight in the evening, a German submarine, U-30, under a young commander named Fritz-Julius Lemp, fires a single torpedo into her port side. The Athenia takes most of the night to sink. Lemp has mistaken the liner, in the failing light, for a British armed merchant cruiser. By the morning, when other ships arrive to take off the survivors, one hundred and twelve passengers are dead, including twenty-eight Americans. The first ship to be sunk in the Battle of the Atlantic, on the first day, has carried civilians.

We put a great deal of care into bringing you these long stories. If you have settled in and you are enjoying this, a quiet like helps the channel reach more people who like to fall asleep to history, and subscribing tells us to keep producing them. Thank you for staying with us.

In Berlin, the news of the Athenia is at first treated as an embarrassment. The German naval high command, under Grand Admiral Erich Raeder, has been told by the Foreign Ministry that the war will be a limited European affair and that British shipping is not to be attacked without warning. Lemp's mistake is therefore, officially, not his. The U-30's log is altered. The German press is told that the British have sunk their own ship as a propaganda trick. Lemp himself is privately reprimanded and sent back to sea. He will go on, in October, to lay mines off the British south coast and, in May of nineteen forty-one, to be killed in the action that surrenders his next boat, U-110, and her Enigma machine, to the Royal Navy. But that is much further down the road tonight.

Three days after the Athenia, on the seventeenth of September, the British aircraft carrier Courageous, on submarine patrol off the Hebrides, is torpedoed and sunk by U-29 in twenty minutes, with the loss of five hundred and nineteen of her crew. The Royal Navy quickly stops using its valuable carriers in such a role. Then, on the night of the thirteenth and fourteenth of October, a small skilled commander named Günther Prien, in U-47, threads his boat through the eastern entrance of the great British naval anchorage at Scapa Flow, in the Orkney Islands, and torpedoes the battleship Royal Oak at her mooring. The old battleship rolls over and sinks in twelve minutes with the loss of eight hundred and thirty-three men, more than a third of her crew. Prien returns to the German port of Wilhelmshaven and is decorated personally by Hitler. He becomes the first national hero of the German U-boat arm. He has eighteen months to live.

Through the winter of nineteen thirty-nine into nineteen forty, the Atlantic war is, in volume, still small. The German U-boat fleet under Admiral Karl Dönitz numbers fewer than sixty boats, of which only about thirty are ocean-going and only eight or nine can be on station in the Atlantic at any one time. They sink merchantmen by submerged torpedo attack and by deck-gun action against unescorted ships, working from bases on the German North Sea coast. The British, meanwhile, gather their merchantmen into convoys, escorted by elderly destroyers and a growing number of Flower-class corvettes, small whaler-derived ships built quickly in commercial yards. The escorts are equipped with asdic, the underwater detection set the Americans will later call sonar, and depth charges, and very little else.

In the spring of nineteen forty, the war on land changes the Atlantic war forever. In April, German forces invade Norway and Denmark. In May, they sweep through the Low Countries and into France. By the end of June, France has surrendered. The German navy now holds, at a stroke, the entire Atlantic coast from northern Norway down through Denmark, the Low Countries, and the long western face of France itself. The U-boats move into the new bases at Brest, at Lorient, at Saint-Nazaire, at La Pallice, at Bordeaux, with their long concrete pens being built that summer by the Todt construction organization, walls thick enough to defy any bomb the Allies will have for the next two years. The transit time from base to convoy lanes, which had been ten or twelve days from Germany, now becomes three or four. The U-boats double their effective time on station overnight. The men of the boats begin to call the next year the Glückliche Zeit. The Happy Time.

Through the autumn of nineteen forty and into nineteen forty-one, a small group of U-boat commanders becomes very famous very quickly. Otto Kretschmer, in U-99, perfects the night surface attack: bring the boat in low on the surface, use her small silhouette and a cold engine exhaust against the dark water, fire torpedoes into the lighter sky behind the convoy, and slip out at speed. He sinks more tonnage than any other commander of the war. Joachim Schepke, in U-100, attacks the same way, with flair and very little caution. Prien, in U-47, becomes the most famous, the man who took Royal Oak. They wear white caps in port and write self-confident dispatches at sea. They are sometimes joined for sortie or evening on board the headquarters yacht of the U-boat command, in the small French port of Kernevel, where a stocky, careful officer named Dönitz is running the entire campaign from a chart-strewn study on the second floor.

Dönitz himself has fought as a U-boat officer in the First World War. He believes, with great conviction, that the Atlantic war can be won by sinking merchant tonnage faster than the Allies can build it, and that the right way to do this is the wolf pack — Rudeltaktik — in which a line of U-boats spread across the convoy lanes will, on first contact, radio a sighting report to Kernevel, where Dönitz himself or his staff will direct the other boats in the line to converge on the convoy and attack on the surface at night. The wolf pack, as it works through the autumn of nineteen forty, can devastate a convoy. In October, in three nights of running battle, two convoys, SC-7 and HX-79, lose thirty-two ships between them to a pack of seven U-boats. There is a moment, in the British Admiralty in the autumn of forty, when the situation on paper looks very dark. Imports of food and oil and raw materials are running below the level the country needs to keep eating and keep making weapons. Churchill will say, after the war, that the only thing that ever really frightened him during the war was the U-boat peril. He is speaking of these months and of the fifteen months that follow.

The great change of nineteen forty-one is not a single event but a slow accumulation. In March of that year, in a single ten-day stretch in the western approaches, three of the famous aces are taken out at once. Prien is lost with all hands when U-47 is sunk in a depth-charge attack by the destroyer Wolverine on the seventh of March. A week later, on the night of the sixteenth, Kretschmer in U-99 and Schepke in U-100 attack convoy HX-112 together. Schepke is rammed and crushed in his own conning tower by the destroyer Vanoc. Kretschmer's U-99 is depth-charged to the surface by the destroyer Walker, which lifts her crew out of the water as the boat sinks under them. Kretschmer himself spends the rest of the war as a prisoner in Canada, where he plays bridge with American officers and writes letters home. The German U-boat arm has lost, in three days, the three commanders most closely associated in the public mind with the Happy Time. The youngest officers who are now coming into the boats will not remember an Atlantic in which the U-boat had this kind of advantage.

The technological war is also tilting, although neither side knows it fully yet. In May of nineteen forty-one, an alert British escort group commander named Joe Baker-Cresswell, in the destroyer Bulldog, depth-charges a U-boat, U-110, to the surface near Iceland. The crew abandons the boat and the British, instead of letting it sink, send a boarding party across by whaler. They go down inside the still-floating hull, and they take out the boat's intact four-rotor Enigma cipher machine, its current settings, and its codebooks. The capture is treated with the most absolute secrecy. The U-110 is later allowed to sink under tow, and the German navy is told only that she did not return. From this date forward, with a delay of weeks at first and later only of hours, the British codebreakers at Bletchley Park, north of London — under the direction of a quiet mathematician named Alan Turing and his colleagues — read the operational radio traffic of the German Atlantic U-boats. They learn where the wolf packs are positioned, what their next contact line will be, where the empty water is. The information is given the codename Ultra, and it is fed quietly into the Operations Intelligence Centre in the basement of the Admiralty in London. There, on a great plotting table, a team led by a meticulous officer named Rodger Winn moves small wooden markers each watch, marking the daily position of every known U-boat in the Atlantic. The convoy routing officer in the next room then plots the eastbound and westbound convoys to thread between them. Sometimes a convoy passes through fog. Sometimes it does not. The system is never perfect. But the wolf packs no longer find every convoy.

In the same May of nineteen forty-one, the surface war comes briefly to the Atlantic. The new German battleship Bismarck, fifty thousand tons of armor and fifteen-inch guns, slips out of Bergen with the heavy cruiser Prinz Eugen for a commerce raid into the western Atlantic. On the morning of the twenty-fourth, in the Denmark Strait between Iceland and Greenland, she meets the British battlecruiser Hood and the new battleship Prince of Wales. Hood is hit by Bismarck's third or fourth salvo, blows up amidships, and sinks in three minutes with the loss of fourteen hundred and fifteen of her crew. There are three survivors. The British Home Fleet, including the carrier Victorious and the carrier Ark Royal up from Gibraltar, gives chase across the Atlantic for three days. On the evening of the twenty-sixth of May, an old Swordfish biplane from Ark Royal puts a torpedo into Bismarck's stern and jams her steering gear. She circles helplessly through the night under the lash of the gale. On the morning of the twenty-seventh, the British battleships Rodney and King George the Fifth come up and pound her into a wreck. Bismarck sinks, with two thousand of her crew aboard. The film of these days is made many times in the years that follow. The wider war, meanwhile, has gone on. The convoys are still sailing. The U-boats are still at sea.

Later that summer, in August nineteen forty-one, Roosevelt and Churchill meet at sea in Placentia Bay, off Newfoundland, aboard the heavy cruiser Augusta and the battleship Prince of Wales. They sign the Atlantic Charter, a brief eight-point statement of war aims that includes self-determination, freedom of the seas, and disarmament of aggressor nations after the war. The United States is not yet in the war. Roosevelt has been moving, however, very steadily toward it. In September, after a U-boat fires torpedoes at the American destroyer Greer (which had been chasing it on behalf of British forces), Roosevelt declares a shoot-on-sight policy in the western Atlantic. American destroyers begin escorting Allied convoys as far east as Iceland. In October, the American destroyer Reuben James, of an old four-stack Wickes class, is torpedoed and sunk by U-552 west of Iceland with the loss of one hundred and fifteen men. The American public reads about it in the morning papers. The country is at war in everything but name.

Then comes Pearl Harbor and the formal American declaration. And then, six weeks later, comes a second Happy Time for the U-boats, this one off the American eastern seaboard.

Dönitz had foreseen, when the United States declared war in December nineteen forty-one, that there would be, for a few weeks, a window of opportunity along the American coast. The American navy and merchant marine had not yet learned the convoy lessons that the British had learned at such cost over the previous two years. Coastal cities still kept their lights on at night, silhouetting the merchant ships passing them on the lighter horizon. Coastal shipping still ran independently and at advertised speeds and routes. Dönitz called the operation he ordered against this coast Paukenschlag — the Drumbeat. The first wave was only five Type IX long-range U-boats. They began arriving off the New York and North Carolina approaches in mid-January nineteen forty-two.

What followed, through the first months of nineteen forty-two, was one of the worst defeats the merchant marine of any nation has ever suffered. In January and February alone, the U-boats sank more than eighty ships in American coastal waters. The waters off Cape Hatteras became known to the U-boat crews as the American shooting grounds. Tankers carrying Caribbean oil were torpedoed within sight of the Florida hotels, with their lights still burning, and tourists came down to the beach in the morning to find oil and bodies in the sand. American naval reaction, under Admiral Ernest King at the Navy Department in Washington, was slow. King, an austere man who did not like the British, was reluctant to accept the convoy advice that the British were freely offering. Coastal blackouts were not imposed on Miami until April. A coastal interlocking convoy system was not in place until late May. By the time the Americans had their coastal waters under control, in the summer of nineteen forty-two, more than six hundred Allied ships had been sunk in American waters. The U-boats, who had been running short on torpedoes and supplies, had been replenished by purpose-built supply submarines they called Milchkühe, milk cows, working in mid-Atlantic. The crews who returned from these patrols brought home oranges and steaks and silk stockings and fresh memories of the lights of Atlantic City still burning at midnight. Dönitz, in his quiet study at Kernevel, told his diary that the second Happy Time had been even better than the first.

By the autumn of nineteen forty-two, the U-boat campaign returns to its center of gravity, the mid-North Atlantic, where the great convoys move between Halifax and Liverpool and between Sydney, Cape Breton, and the Mersey. The U-boat fleet has grown enormously. By the end of the year, Dönitz has more than three hundred U-boats in commission, with up to a hundred at sea on any given day. The wolf packs, sometimes twenty boats long, are stretched across the convoy lanes like a curtain. Many convoys pass through them undetected, thanks to Ultra. Many do not. Through the autumn and winter of forty-two and into the spring of forty-three, the convoy battles in the mid-Atlantic become, for the men in the small escort ships and the merchantmen, the long bitter heart of the war.

The great problem, in those months, is the air-cover gap. Long-range patrol aircraft from Iceland and from the British Isles can cover the eastern part of the route. Long-range patrol aircraft from Newfoundland and from Greenland can cover the western part. But there is, in the middle of the ocean, a wedge of water perhaps six hundred miles across, south and east of Greenland, that cannot yet be reached by any patrol aircraft based on land. The men of the convoys call it the Air Gap, the Black Pit, or simply the Gap. In the Gap, the U-boats run on the surface in daylight, charge their batteries, and move at sixteen knots, faster than any escort except the destroyers. In the Gap, the wolf pack tactic works. Outside it, with patrol aircraft overhead, the U-boats must dive when sighted, and once submerged they make only a few knots, slower than any convoy.

In early March of nineteen forty-three, the Gap produces its great battle. The slow eastbound convoy SC-122, of fifty merchantmen, and the faster eastbound convoy HX-229, of forty merchantmen, are at sea on overlapping tracks. A wolf pack of seventeen U-boats, called Raubgraf and later combined with two further packs, finds first one and then the other. Over the course of three days and nights, from the sixteenth to the nineteenth of March, in a continuous running battle in cold green seas, twenty-two merchant ships and one escort destroyer are sunk for the loss of one U-boat. The losses send a shudder through the Admiralty. The official British naval staff history will say later, with restraint, that it appeared possible the Germans could deny us the use of the Atlantic. For the men who made the convoys go through, the same idea had a less restrained name. They called it, in the spring of nineteen forty-three, the crisis.

The crisis lasts only a few weeks. By April and May of nineteen forty-three, almost everything in the Atlantic war that had been moving in the direction of victory at last lands.

The Royal Air Force Coastal Command, under Air Marshal John Slessor, has been receiving very-long-range Liberator bombers, modified American B-24s with extra fuel tanks in the bomb bays. By the spring of nineteen forty-three, three squadrons of these aircraft, flying from Northern Ireland and from Iceland and from Newfoundland, can finally close the air gap. Anywhere a U-boat surfaces in the North Atlantic, an aircraft can be there within a few hours.

The convoys themselves now have escort carriers — small American-built ships of fifteen thousand tons, with flight decks long enough for a dozen Avenger and Wildcat aircraft, sailing as part of the escort group itself. The first of them, USS Bogue and HMS Biter, are at sea by the spring of nineteen forty-three. They give continuous local air cover whether or not a land-based aircraft can reach the convoy.

The escorts have new weapons. The Hedgehog, a forward-throwing twenty-four-bomb mortar fitted to the foredeck, allows a corvette or destroyer to keep its asdic contact during the attack run, instead of running over the U-boat at the last moment with stern depth charges and losing the contact. The Squid, which arrives later, fires three full-sized depth charges in a triangle ahead of the ship. The Mark Twenty-four passive acoustic homing torpedo, called Fido by its American crews, can be dropped by an aircraft into the swirl where a U-boat has dived, and will run a slow circular pattern listening for the sound of the screws. It works.

The escorts also have, by the spring of nineteen forty-three, high-frequency direction finding gear, called Huff-Duff by the men who use it. Whenever a U-boat sends a sighting report or a position report to Kernevel, the Huff-Duff sets on the convoy escort ships take a near-instantaneous bearing on her, and pairs of escorts can triangulate her position within a few miles. The U-boat, which has assumed all winter that her radio transmissions are anonymous, has been giving away her position with every signal.

And the codebreakers at Bletchley Park, who had lost their reading of the four-rotor naval Enigma in February nineteen forty-two when the Germans introduced the Triton variant, have got it back. In December nineteen forty-two, after a year of darkness, with the help of three new high-speed code-breaking machines called bombes, designed in part by Turing's group, Bletchley reads Triton again. Through the spring of forty-three, the British and Canadian and American navies know, again, where most of the wolf packs are positioned each day.

All these things come together in the month that the U-boat sailors will, afterward, call Schwarzer Mai. Black May. In May of nineteen forty-three, in convoy battles around ONS-5 and SC-130 and HX-237, in mid-Atlantic engagements with combined Allied surface and air, forty-one U-boats are sunk. The Allied losses are heavy enough — twenty-two ships from ONS-5 alone — but they are within the levels the Allied building yards can replace. The U-boat losses are not. Dönitz, who has just taken over the entire German navy from Raeder as Grand Admiral, recognizes by the end of the month that his men cannot continue. On the twenty-fourth of May, he orders all U-boats to withdraw from the North Atlantic convoy lanes and to refit and retrain. The decision is the end of the wolf-pack era. The U-boats will return, but they will never again be the strategic threat that they were in March nineteen forty-three.

Through the summer and autumn of nineteen forty-three, the Allies pursue. American escort carrier groups, the hunter-killer groups, work in the central Atlantic, attacking the supply submarines and the boats refueling from them. The supply submarines, the milk cows, are sunk one by one. By the autumn there are no more, and the long-range U-boats can no longer remain on station for the full eight or ten weeks that earlier patrols had managed. RAF Coastal Command opens an offensive in the Bay of Biscay, the body of water that every U-boat from the French ports must cross on its way to and from sea. Liberators, Halifaxes, Sunderlands, Wellingtons of Coastal Command fly day-and-night sorties over the Bay, with new ten-centimeter radar that the U-boats cannot detect. Through the summer of nineteen forty-three, U-boats begin to be lost in numbers in the Bay itself, before they have ever reached the open ocean.

The German navy responds with technological adaptations. The schnorchel — a long retractable tube that allows a U-boat to run her diesels and charge her batteries while remaining submerged at periscope depth — is fitted to most boats from the spring of nineteen forty-four. It nearly halves the average speed of a patrol but it allows the boat to remain underwater for weeks at a time, and it makes life inside the boats grim and damp and oxygen-starved. The Type XXI, a revolutionary design with a streamlined hull and electric drive that can run submerged at seventeen knots and stay down for days, is laid down in nineteen forty-three and ordered into mass production by prefabricated section. The Type XXIII, a smaller coastal version, is also rushed forward. Both are real technological advances. Both come too late. By the spring of nineteen forty-five, only a handful of Type XXIs and Type XXIIIs have made operational patrols, and only one or two have sunk a ship. The war ends before the elektroboot can change the balance.

In the same months, on the British side, a particular kind of officer comes into his own. The Western Approaches Tactical Unit, set up the year before in a basement room in Liverpool by Admiral Sir Max Horton and a young Wren officer named Jean Laidlaw, has been training escort group commanders on a great chequered linoleum floor, with junior officers playing both the U-boats and the merchant ships, and with simulated radar plots and asdic returns updated by hand. The lessons that come out of this room — to attack the U-boat that has just dived rather than chase the contact-keeper, to keep one ship covering the convoy at all costs, to drill a standard set of hunting maneuvers so that the team can react without signal — are the basis of the doctrine that the escort groups carry into the spring of nineteen forty-three.

The most famous of those commanders is a small wiry captain named Frederic John Walker, who takes command of the Second Support Group in HMS Starling in the spring of nineteen forty-three. Walker had been passed over for promotion before the war and brought back to active service as the Atlantic crisis deepened. His group, working as a free-roving hunter-killer team rather than as escort to a single convoy, sinks more U-boats than any other surface formation of the war. Walker himself is one of those rare men whose presence on a bridge changes the temper of every ship under him. His group plays "A-Hunting We Will Go" over the loud-hailers on the way home from each successful patrol. Walker is decorated four times with the Distinguished Service Order. He works himself, in the literal sense, to death. He dies of exhaustion ashore in July nineteen forty-four, at the age of forty-eight, and is buried at sea from a destroyer in Liverpool Bay. The men of his group, lining the rails for the burial, weep openly. He is remembered, in the small Royal Navy of those years, as the model of what an escort officer could be.

Meanwhile, in the convoy lanes, the merchant ships go on, in numbers that the U-boats can no longer touch. The American Liberty ship program, by the end of nineteen forty-three, is producing one new dry-cargo merchantman every twelve hours from yards in Baltimore, in Portland Maine, in Mobile, in Houston, in Richmond California, in Brunswick Georgia. Welded together from prefabricated sections by men and women of every age, including women who had never worked in a shipyard before in their lives, the Liberties are not beautiful, but they are enough. By the end of the war, more than two thousand seven hundred of them have been launched. Their replacement rate is so high that the U-boats simply cannot sink them faster than they can be built. The same is true, with smaller numbers, of the British and Canadian merchant programs, of the new escort destroyers and frigates and corvettes, of the long American escort carrier program. The arithmetic, by the autumn of forty-three, is in the Allies' favor.

In the spring and summer of nineteen forty-four, the convoy effort feeds the great invasion of Europe. In the months before D-Day, the Atlantic carries to Britain not only the food and oil that keep the country running, but also the great accumulating weight of the American expeditionary force — two million men, a hundred thousand vehicles, fuel and ammunition for an army that will fight from Normandy to the Elbe. The U-boats try to interfere. Boats with the new schnorchel are sent into the English Channel and the western approaches, in the early summer of nineteen forty-four, in a desperate effort to attack the invasion shipping. They sink a few ships. They are themselves sunk in numbers, by escorts and by Coastal Command aircraft. By the late summer of forty-four, the German army's collapse in France leads to the loss of the great U-boat bases — Brest, Lorient, Saint-Nazaire, La Pallice. The boats that can still get to sea move to bases in Norway, in Trondheim and Bergen and Narvik. The transit time to the Atlantic doubles again. The patrols become shorter, the kills fewer.

Through the winter of nineteen forty-four to forty-five, the U-boats fight on. With the schnorchel, they hunt close to the British coast, in the western approaches, in the Irish Sea, in the English Channel itself. They sink coastal merchantmen, occasional larger vessels, an LST off the southwest English coast in March. The losses to the boats themselves remain heavy. The Germans go on building. By April nineteen forty-five there are still nearly a hundred and fifty U-boats at sea or ready for sea. Most of them never sail again.

On the thirtieth of April nineteen forty-five, with Soviet armies in the Berlin streets, Hitler kills himself in his bunker beneath the chancellery. Grand Admiral Dönitz, by the terms of Hitler's last political testament, is named the new head of state. From his small headquarters in Plön, in the north of Germany, in the first days of May, Dönitz negotiates the surrender of all German forces in the west. On the fourth of May, German forces in northwestern Europe surrender to Field Marshal Montgomery on Lüneburg Heath. On the seventh of May, Dönitz authorizes the general unconditional surrender, which is signed at Eisenhower's headquarters in Reims and at Marshal Zhukov's headquarters in Berlin. The cease-fire takes effect at one minute past midnight on the ninth of May.

For the U-boats, the order to cease hostilities is broadcast on the eighth of May. The signal, sent on the long German naval frequencies, is short. Boats at sea are told to surface, fly a black flag, broadcast their positions in plain language, jettison ammunition, sail to designated Allied ports, and surrender. Most do. In the western approaches and the Irish Sea, in the bay of Biscay, in the central Atlantic, in the Indian Ocean, in the Caribbean, U-boat after U-boat surfaces and signals. They are met, often within a few hours, by Allied warships and aircraft. The Allied crews look down on them from their bridges. The German crews stand on their narrow casings in their leather jackets, blinking in the daylight. There are exceptions. A handful of boats refuse to surrender and either scuttle themselves or, in two famous cases, run all the way to Argentina, where they put in months later and are interned. But almost all of them come in.

In the weeks that follow, more than one hundred and fifty U-boats are gathered in British and Canadian ports, mainly Loch Ryan in Scotland and Lisahally in Northern Ireland. After being inspected and stripped of useful equipment, most of them are towed out to a deep area of the Atlantic west of the Hebrides and sunk by gunfire and by air-dropped torpedoes, in an operation called Deadlight. One hundred and sixteen boats are sent to the bottom in this way through the autumn and early winter of nineteen forty-five. They lie now in twelve thousand feet of water, in the dark cold of the deep ocean.

The long Battle of the Atlantic, in the final accounting, has been the longest battle of the Second World War. It has lasted from the first hours of the third of September nineteen thirty-nine to the last hours of the eighth of May nineteen forty-five — five years and eight months. In that time, three thousand five hundred Allied merchant ships have been lost, and one hundred and seventy-five Allied warships of various sizes. Some thirty thousand Allied merchant seamen have died in the cold water, a higher percentage of dead per service than any uniformed branch of any of the Western nations. On the German side, of the forty thousand men who served in the U-boat arm, about twenty-eight thousand are dead, and another five thousand are prisoners. The U-boat arm has the highest casualty rate of any service in any major nation in the war. Of seven hundred and ninety U-boats sent on operational war patrols, seven hundred and eighty-three are sunk or scuttled. The aces — Prien and Schepke and Endrass and many of the others — lie under the cold green water with their boats. Kretschmer, who survived, returns home from Canadian captivity, becomes a small ship's broker in Hamburg, and finally a NATO admiral in the West German navy of the nineteen sixties, before retiring quietly to a house on a lake in Bavaria. He outlives all the others. He dies in nineteen ninety-eight.

The ocean itself, over the years, returns to its normal traffic. The convoys disperse in the summer of forty-five. Their ships go back to private companies and resume the routes they had run before the war. The escort carriers are sold to civilian use, where most of them are converted into coastal freighters or scrapped within a few years. The frigates and corvettes go to reserve or to friendly navies. Bletchley Park is closed up for thirty years, and the men and women who worked there go home and tell no one what they did, including in many cases their husbands and wives, until the secret is finally lifted in nineteen seventy-four, when many of them are old or already dead.

The great convoy ports are quiet. Halifax, in Nova Scotia, where so many ships had loaded and grouped and left, becomes a quiet Maritime city again. Liverpool, on the Mersey, where the convoys came in to the great Gladstone Dock, rebuilds the parts of itself that German bombs had broken in the spring of nineteen forty-one. Saint-Nazaire and Lorient, the great concrete pens of the Atlantic U-boat war, still stand on the French coast, because they are too solid to be cheaply dismantled, and they remain — a museum at Saint-Nazaire, a marine engineering school at Lorient, a memorial at La Rochelle — the most visible ruins of the war.

The sea above the wrecks is, in the end, very quiet. There are some four hundred and sunken U-boats and several thousand sunken merchantmen scattered across the North Atlantic floor. Most of them have never been visited. A few have been found in the last decades by deep-sea expeditions — the Bismarck in nineteen eighty-nine by Robert Ballard's team, four miles down on a soft mud slope; the U-110 a decade later, near where Bulldog had taken her Enigma; some of the convoy victims found by chance in the search for the Titanic. The wrecks lie undisturbed in cold black water. Their hulls slowly rust. The plankton drift down through the dark water above them, in the long fall that biologists call the marine snow, settling at last on the rusting steel.

This is the long Battle of the Atlantic, told as gently as it can be told. The first night and the Athenia. The Royal Oak in Scapa Flow. The fall of France and the move into Lorient. The Happy Time and the three aces lost in three days. The Bismarck and the Enigma machine taken from U-110. The American coast and the lights of Atlantic City. The Black Pit and the convoy crisis of March forty-three. Black May. The closing of the Bay of Biscay. The schnorchel boats in the western approaches. The black flags raised in May forty-five. The hundred and sixteen boats sunk in Operation Deadlight in the deep Atlantic west of the Hebrides.

The ocean, after all of this, runs in its long swells, east to west and west to east, as it always has. Tonight, somewhere out there, a freighter is moving across the empty mid-Atlantic, with a single small lamp burning on her bridge, and the same long dark water below her that the corvettes once watched from their open bridge wings, and the same small pinpricks of starlight that the U-boat lookouts once watched, in their wet leather jackets, from their narrow steel conning towers. The ships are no longer at war. The seas are no longer dangerous in that particular way. The cold dark water has gone back to being only itself. The men who fought it have grown old and most of them are gone, on every side. The wrecks lie quiet on the deep mud. The waves above them go on, in their steady patient rhythm, year after year, as if the war had never been there at all.

We put a great deal of effort into bringing you this. If it has helped you rest, a quiet like helps the channel, and subscribing tells us to keep making more long, soft histories like this one. Thank you for staying with us tonight. Sleep well.
